1:
Who is being called is the first question. Gill reports the Jewish commentators taking the address to the Gentiles, and agrees, their conversion being plainly spoken of. Henry widens it: not the Jews only, but whoever can be picked up out of the highways and hedges, since the gospel covenant excludes none who do not exclude themselves. Ellicott hears something gentler, an invitation addressed in a tone of pity to the bereaved woman of the preceding chapter. On the one qualification they agree. Henry says all are welcome to grace on the single condition that grace be welcome to them, and where God gives it he first gives a thirsting after it; Wesley calls the thirst vehement.

The waters are read three ways. Henry takes them commercially, sending the hearer to the quays where foreign goods are landed, which would have stayed foreign for ever had Christ not brought in an everlasting righteousness. Clarke reports a Jewish reading in which water stands for the law and wisdom, without which the world could no more subsist than without water, wine because it rejoices the heart and milk because it nourishes a child. Ellicott keeps all three as symbols of spiritual blessing, and notes that the verb rendered buy is elsewhere confined to corn.

That verb has to be defended against itself. Ellicott observes that the prophet, having said buy, feels it may be misunderstood, and adds that no silver can purchase what is offered; something is required, which is why buy stays the right word, but the price is the self-surrender that accepts the blessing. Wesley gets there sooner, glossing it as receiving what is freely given, and adding that the most worthless are welcome if they do but thirst. On what is wasted instead they divide: Gill takes the money spent on what is not bread for strength given to false doctrine, while Wesley reads it of worldly goods and pleasures.

Clarke asks, in Gill's vein, why men are so zealously attached to a doctrine from which their souls derive neither comfort nor nourishment. Ellicott takes the labour for its earnings, spent on not-bread by a people now called to take the true bread for not-money, which he explains as the simple hearing of faith, and reads the fatness as the exuberance of spiritual joy. On the promise that the soul shall live he prefers revive, a waking to new life, and Keil and Delitzsch render it so too, adding that what is offered is superabundance rather than the bare satisfaction of need.

The covenant divides them. Clarke renders the verb as cutting a covenant sacrifice, and identifies it with the sacrifice pointed out from the beginning, the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world. Ellicott takes it for the new covenant, the expansion and completion of the one made with David as representative of the true King, whom the prophet now treats as identical with the servant of the Lord, and would render the sure mercies as the unfailing loving-kindnesses. Wesley traces it back to the covenant made first with Abraham and afterwards with David, and says David here seems put for the son of David.

On the witness given to the peoples the split is clean. Gill takes it for the Messiah and refers the giving to an act past in eternity, when Christ was appointed Mediator; Wesley likewise makes him the David last mentioned. Ellicott would render it I gave, referring the words primarily to the historic David, realised fully only in the one called the faithful and true witness. The last verse turns outward. Gill describes the called nation as aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and notes the paradox that those God knows as his own are unknown to him before their calling. Ellicott sees the calling of the Gentiles and the expansion of the true idea of Israel.
6:
The little word while carries the weight of the verse, and one voice refuses it. Clarke reports a Jewish commentator he credits with the true sense, reading the clauses as causal rather than temporal: seek the Lord because he may be found, call upon him because he is near, and repent before you die, for after death there is no conversion of the soul. The others keep the limit. Ellicott says the appeal shows the promised blessings are not unconditional, and a time may come when too late is written across every effort to recover an inheritance forfeited by neglect. Wesley reads it of the day of grace, while mercy is still offered. Henry takes both halves: now God's patience waits and his Spirit strives, but a day comes when he is afar off and not found.

Henry adds that such a day may arrive within this life, when the heart is incurably hardened, and at death the door is certainly shut. He divides the summons into two duties. To seek the Lord is to enquire of him as one's oracle and seek him as one's happiness, sorry to have lost him and solicitous to find him, taking the appointed method by making Christ the way, the Spirit the guide and the word the rule. To call upon him is to pray first to be reconciled and then, being reconciled, for everything else one needs. Wesley puts it in a line: seeking means labouring to know God's will and obtain his grace, and near means ready and desirous to receive.

What the wicked man must forsake is his way, and Gill offers two senses of it. It is his own way in the plain sense, of his own choosing and delight, so dangerous that nothing but efficacious grace will turn him from it, and forsaken only when he sees its evil. But it may also mean his own way of saving himself, by works of righteousness he has done, set in opposition to God's way. Henry insists the forsaking must go deeper than conduct, since the verse names thoughts too: there must be not only a change of way but a change of mind, and it is not enough to break off evil practices without entering a caveat against evil thoughts. Wesley compresses the whole to sincere repentance and faith.

The reason then given is the distance between the two minds, and each takes it somewhere different. Gill works it as a comparison: thoughts are natural to God and man alike, internal and unknown until made known, but man's are finite and have a beginning where God's have none; and it is the quality more than the nature that is meant, since men's thoughts are evil and vain and God's holy. Ellicott refers the assertion to promise and warning together, and names the human thoughts contradicted: that the gifts of God can be bought with money and that the market where they are sold is always open. Wesley narrows it to pardon, contrasting our slowness to forgive a man who injures us often with God's readiness to forgive all penitents however many their sins.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the appeal as urged on a heaven-wide difference between God's ways and both the despairing thoughts of men and their aimless labyrinthine ways, the particle introducing a fact patent to the senses in order to set the comparison out plainly. Gill says only that no greater distance can be conceived than that of the heavens above the earth. Clarke finds a defect in the text here, suspecting the small particle of comparison has been lost through its likeness to the particle immediately before it; all the ancient versions express it, and he supports the conjecture from a psalm saying nearly the same thing in nearly the same words.
10:
The rain figure is handled with different degrees of allegory. Gill keeps to the natural fact and adds a qualification the verse does not make: rain and snow do not return until they have done what they were sent to do, though they may afterwards be exhaled into vapours and drawn up by the sun. Wesley notices that the snow has its season and contributes in it to the earth's fruitfulness, and that the bread-corn serves twice, for present supply and for next year's seed. Ellicott finds the whole apparatus of the agricultural parables present here: the rain and dew the gracious influences that prepare the heart, the seed the divine word, the sower the Servant of the Lord, the bread the fruits of holiness that sustain the life of others.

What the word is that goes out of the mouth divides even a single commentator. Gill offers two readings and does not choose between them. It may be Christ the eternal Word, who came down from heaven as rain does, suddenly and freely and with great efficacy, watering his people through the ministry of the word, and who returned to heaven but not empty, having gathered a harvest and accomplished the whole pleasure of God. Or it may be the word of promise, which is made in heaven and comes down from it in the same manner. Wesley takes the narrower of the two and specifies the content, that the promises meant are those concerning the pardon of the greatest sinners.

Where the point of the comparison lies is a genuine disagreement. Keil and Delitzsch locate it in energy: the true likeness is the force with which the word is realised, and the word of redemption will be fulfilled irresistibly. Ellicott locates it in proportion. What the natural world shows is the predominance of fertility despite partial or apparent failures, and that is the pledge of a like triumph in the long run of God's purposes over man's resistance. He then draws the consequence that distinguishes his reading, and does not soften it: the comparison does not exclude the partial or even total failure of many, and what it asserts is that the saved are more than the lost.

On the singing of the hills two reach independently for the same classical parallel, a passage in which the unshorn mountains fling their voices to the stars and the rocks sound with them. Clarke quotes it in a rendering that has the mountain tops rejoice and the shrubs partake of human voice; Ellicott quotes the same lines in a version that has the hills break forth to the stars in minstrelsies, and adds what makes the image exact, that the waving of branches is to a tree what the clapping of hands is to a man. Wesley says the rejoicing is general, so that even the senseless creatures seem to rejoice with them. Gill allows that the going out may literally mean the return from captivity.

The thorn and the fir are read morally by all of them. Gill takes the briers for wicked men, fruitless and harmful and destined to be burned, and the fir and myrtle for good men, the change being fulfilled when the gospel was preached in the Gentile world. Clarke calls them general poetical images of a great and happy change, the wilderness turned into a paradise and the desert of the Gentiles watered by the same heavenly rain, and reports the old Aramaic version giving the moral sense outright: instead of the wicked shall arise the just, and instead of sinners such as fear to sin. He notes that a conjunction attested by many manuscripts and every ancient version was left in the margin rather than the text, and remarks that the best reading is very often found there. Wesley takes the sign for a monument to later generations.
